176.title: Az-Zalzalah: the quake
176.hook: on that Day the earth tells its news, and an atom's weight of good is seen (Surah 99)
176.howItsDone: Az-Zalzalah is recited in the prayers, and its last two verses on the atom's weight of good and ill are among the most quoted lines in Muslim teaching on small deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Adiyat, the chargers, and the human who forgets his blessings. Your line was gratitude charges forward. Who did you thank that you'd taken for granted? Day one hundred seventy-six.

People who've lived through an earthquake describe the same thing first. Not the noise. The ground. The one thing you never think about, the thing that holds everything up, suddenly moving under your feet. Glasses rattle, then walls, and the floor feels like the deck of a boat. Everything you assumed was solid isn't. Today's surah opens with the whole earth shaking like that, once and for all. And then it does something tender: it zooms all the way down, to the smallest thing there is. Today: Az-Zalzalah, the quake.
screen: `THE GROUND MOVES UNDER YOU.` → `NOTHING SOLID IS SOLID.` → `THEN, THE SMALLEST THING.`

segments.voice: Zalzalah is a word that shakes when you say it: zal-zala, the syllables doubling like a tremor. The surah begins: when the earth is shaken with its final quake, and throws out its burdens, and a person asks, what's wrong with it? That day it will tell its news. We'll come back to that line tomorrow. Today, the ending, which many Muslims know by heart. In Pickthall's translation: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then. The word translated atom is dharrah. In the Arabic of the time it meant a tiny ant, or a speck of dust in a sunbeam, the smallest thing a person could see. In the surah's picture, nothing gets lost. Not the big donation, and not the smile at the cashier. Not the cruel comment, and not the kind one. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made the same point in a hadith in Bukhari: protect yourself from the Fire, even with half a date given in charity. Half a date. And in Muslim: don't look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. This surah is where the stretch we've been reading, from the last page of the Qur'an backward, turns a corner. Eighteen days of the shortest surahs, from An-Nas to here. From tomorrow the surahs grow a little longer. It ends on the right note: an atom of good, seen.
screen: `ZALZALAH — A WORD THAT SHAKES.` · `THE EARTH THROWS OUT ITS BURDENS.` · `DHARRAH — A TINY ANT, A SPECK OF DUST.` · `EVEN HALF A DATE.` · then, large: `AN ATOM OF GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one atom's weight of good. Sit, and picture a dharrah: one speck of dust turning in a sunbeam. Then think that small. Not a big project. One tiny good you can do in the next hour: a glass of water for someone, a kind reply, picking up one piece of litter, a smile on purpose. Picture yourself doing it. Make it so small you can't say no. The bell holds the time.
Az-Zalzalah. The quake, the final shaking of the earth, and the surah that says an atom's weight of good will be seen. Today's word.
Your line: an atom of good. Do one atom's weight of good today, so small it almost doesn't count. The surah says it does. Day one hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 176 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AZ-ZALZALAH AGAIN: THE EARTH'S REPORT.`

177.title: Az-Zalzalah again: the earth's report
177.hook: the ground itself will tell what was done on it (99:4–5)
177.howItsDone: Some Muslims pray their voluntary prayers in a different spot from the obligatory ones, and scholars have connected the practice with the earth bearing witness on the Day of Judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Az-Zalzalah, the quake, and the atom's weight. Your line was an atom of good. What was the tiny good you did, the one so small it almost didn't count? Day one hundred seventy-seven.

Archaeologists can read a floor. Dig down through a site, and the dirt tells you who lived there, what they ate, where they cooked, when the fire came. A footprint in dried mud can last thousands of years. The ground keeps records nobody asked it to keep. Yesterday we heard the end of Surah az-Zalzalah. Today we go back to the line in the middle, the one we skipped, about the earth itself as a witness. And a new stretch of the path begins: the middle surahs, a little longer, a little deeper. Today: Az-Zalzalah again, the earth's report.
screen: `ARCHAEOLOGISTS READ A FLOOR.` → `THE GROUND KEEPS RECORDS.` → `THE MIDDLE SURAHS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: The surah says that on that Day, after the quake, the earth speaks. In Pickthall's translation: That day she will relate her chronicles, Because thy Lord inspireth her. Chronicles, akhbar: news, reports, the story of what happened. The earth, which everyone has walked on, will give its account. How? The surah's answer is simple: because the Lord inspires her, tells her to. A hadith in Tirmidhi fills in the picture. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited this verse and asked his companions: do you know what her news is? They said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: her news is that she will testify about every servant, man or woman, about what they did on her back. She'll say: he did this, on such and such a day. So every place is a witness. The kitchen where you were patient, or weren't. The sidewalk where you stepped around someone, or stopped. The office, the car, the park bench. Scholars drew a gentle conclusion from this, and many Muslims practice it: pray in different places, so more of the earth can speak well of you. Some pray the extra prayers in a different spot from the obligatory ones, partly for this reason. Notice the tone. The ground here isn't an enemy, spying. It's more like an old friend who was there the whole time and remembers. And it can remember good as easily as harm. The ground remembers. So walk as if it does.
screen: `AKHBAR — THE EARTH'S NEWS.` · `BECAUSE THY LORD INSPIRETH HER.` · `SHE TESTIFIES TO WHAT WAS DONE ON HER.` · `PRAY IN MANY PLACES.` · then, large: `THE GROUND REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Stand up if you can, or feel your feet flat on the floor. Notice the ground holding you. Think of this exact spot: what has it seen from you, this week? Then, when the bell ends, take ten slow steps, gently, as if the ground could feel each one and would remember how you walked. If you can't walk, press your feet into the floor softly, ten times. The bell holds the time.
Az-Zalzalah again. The earth's report: on that Day the ground will tell what was done on it. Today's word.
Your line: the ground remembers. Walk gently on the earth today. In one place you pass through, leave something good for it to report. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

178.title: Al-Bayyinah: the clear proof
178.hook: the People of the Book and others awaited a clear sign (Surah 98)
178.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Bayyinah in the prayers, and the hadith of the Prophet reciting it to Ubayy ibn Ka'b is often told as a sign of honor for those who learn and recite the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Az-Zalzalah again, the earth that tells what was done on it. Your line was the ground remembers. Did you walk a little more gently, and where? Day one hundred seventy-eight.

One day, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went to a companion named Ubayy ibn Ka'b, one of the best reciters in Medina, and said something strange. Allah has commanded me to recite to you: those who disbelieve, the opening of Surah al-Bayyinah. Ubayy asked: did He name me? The Prophet said: yes. And Ubayy wept. It's in Sahih al-Bukhari. Imagine being told that the Lord of the worlds said your name. Of all the surahs, this was the one chosen for that moment. Today: Al-Bayyinah, the clear proof.
screen: `RECITE IT TO UBAYY.` → `DID HE NAME ME?` → `AND UBAYY WEPT.`

segments.voice: Bayyinah means a clear proof, evidence you can see, something that makes a matter plain. The root is b-y-n, to be distinct, to stand out clearly, the same root as bayan, a clear statement. The surah opens by describing people waiting. Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, a phrase commentators apply to Jews and Christians, and among the polytheists, the surah says, would not let go of their ways until the clear proof came to them. Then it names that proof: a messenger from Allah, reciting purified pages, containing upright writings. For Muslims, that's the Prophet and the Qur'an he recited. There's a quiet line after that. The surah notes that the People of the Book did not divide until after the clear proof had come to them. Commentators read it as a pattern the Qur'an describes more than once: clarity itself can become the place people disagree. A sign doesn't end argument; sometimes it starts it. The surah then describes, in its closing verses, two kinds of people and their ends, and speaks of those who believe and do good as the best of creation, well pleased with Allah and He with them. Tomorrow we'll hear the verse in the middle, about what was actually asked of everyone. Today, just the word. A clear proof is something that makes things plain enough to choose. The Qur'an presents itself that way: not as a riddle, but as bayyinah, something clear. What people do with clarity is another matter.
screen: `BAYYINAH — EVIDENCE YOU CAN SEE.` · `PEOPLE WAITING FOR A SIGN.` · `A MESSENGER, PURIFIED PAGES.` · `CLARITY CAN BECOME A DISPUTE.` · then, large: `CLEAR PROOF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one clear verse. After this lesson, find one short verse of the Qur'an, from any translation you have, or from a surah you've met here, like by time, or he is one. Read it once, slowly. For now, sit and think of something in your life that is actually clear, that you already know is right, and that you've been putting off anyway. Just let it be plain. The bell holds the time.
Al-Bayyinah. The clear proof, evidence that makes a matter plain; the name of Surah ninety-eight. Today's word.
Your line: clear proof. Today, take one thing you already know clearly is right, and do it, instead of waiting for a bigger sign. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: Al-Bayyinah: sincere devotion
179.hook: all they were asked was to worship Allah sincerely, pray, and give (98:5)
179.howItsDone: Muslims speak of niyyah, intention, before acts of worship, and many recall the hadith 'actions are only by intentions'; Islamic teaching encourages hiding some good deeds so they stay sincere.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Bayyinah, the clear proof, and Ubayy weeping when he heard he'd been named. Your line was clear proof. Did you do one thing you already knew was right? Day one hundred seventy-nine.

Some instructions are long. The tax form, the terms and conditions, the manual for the new washing machine. And some are short enough to write on your hand. Yesterday's surah described people arguing and dividing, even after a clear sign had come. Then, right in the middle, it stops and says, in effect: here's all you were ever asked. One verse. A short list. It's the kind of verse people quote when religion starts to feel complicated. Today: Al-Bayyinah again, sincere devotion.
screen: `SOME INSTRUCTIONS FIT ON YOUR HAND.` → `HERE'S ALL YOU WERE ASKED.` → `ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Verse five of Surah al-Bayyinah, in Pickthall's translation: And they are ordered naught else than to serve Allah, keeping religion pure for Him, as men by nature upright, and to establish worship and to pay the poor-due. Naught else. Nothing more than this. Look at the pieces. First, keeping religion pure for Him. The Arabic is mukhlisin, from the same root as al-Ikhlas, which we met a few weeks ago: sincerity, purity, nothing mixed in. Worship done for Allah, not for an audience, not for a reputation. Second, as men by nature upright: hunafa'. A hanif is someone who turns away from idols toward the one God, and the Qur'an's great example is Ibrahim. It suggests something straight, not bent by pressure. Third and fourth, prayer and giving, salah and zakah, the two practices the Qur'an names together again and again: one toward Allah, one toward people. That's the list. Sincere, upright, praying, giving. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ put the first piece at the head of everything. The very first hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says: actions are only by intentions, and each person gets only what they intended. Two people can do the same prayer, the same donation, side by side, and one did it for Allah and the other did it to be seen. From the outside, identical. Inside, not the same act at all. Sincere and upright. The simplest instruction, and, as anyone who's tried knows, the hardest.
screen: `NAUGHT ELSE — THIS IS ALL.` · `MUKHLISIN — SINCERE, NOTHING MIXED IN.` · `HUNAFA' — UPRIGHT, LIKE IBRAHIM.` · `ACTIONS ARE BY INTENTIONS.` · then, large: `SINCERE AND UPRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one act purely for Allah, or, if that's not your language, purely for the good of it. Something nobody will see or thank you for. Paying for a stranger's coffee without saying so. Cleaning something that isn't yours. Sit now and choose it. Then check your intention honestly: is any part of it for how it looks? If so, make it quieter, until it isn't. The bell holds the time.
Al-Bayyinah. The clear proof, and the surah whose center says: all that was asked is sincere, upright worship, prayer and giving. Today's word.
Your line: sincere and upright. Do one good thing today that no one will ever know about. Keep it that way. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

180.title: Al-Qadr: the Night of Power
180.hook: angels and the Spirit descend, peace until dawn (Surah 97)
180.howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan many Muslims pray late into the night, read Qur'an and make supplication, seeking Laylat al-Qadr in the odd nights; some stay in the mosque in retreat (i'tikaf).

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Bayyinah, and the verse that said all that was asked. Your line was sincere and upright. Did you do one good thing that no one will ever know about? Day one hundred eighty.

Late in Ramadan, in mosques around the world, something changes. The last ten nights, the crowds grow. People who work all day come back at midnight and stay until the pre-dawn meal. Some sleep in the mosque. Children are woken up to join. Everyone is looking for one night, and nobody knows for certain which one it is. Today's surah is five lines about that night: what it is, why it matters, and how it ends. Today: Al-Qadr, the Night of Power.
screen: `THE LAST TEN NIGHTS OF RAMADAN.` → `LOOKING FOR ONE NIGHT.` → `NOBODY KNOWS WHICH.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-seven, in Pickthall's translation: Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power. Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is! The Night of Power is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend therein, by the permission of their Lord, with all decrees. The night is Peace until the rising of the dawn. It is the night the Qur'an was first revealed. Qadr has two meanings, and scholars keep both: power, or honor, greatness; and measure, decree, the night on which matters for the year are measured out. A thousand months is about eighty-three years, longer than most lifetimes. One night, better than a whole life of ordinary nights. The Spirit, ar-ruh, is understood by most commentators to be the angel Jibril, who brought the revelation. So picture the sky that night: full, busy, angels descending. And yet the surah's last word on it isn't noise or power. It's salam. Peace, until the dawn. When is it? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in Bukhari: seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan. Many Muslims especially look to the twenty-seventh, though scholars say it isn't certain, and some say it moves year to year. The uncertainty is part of the gift: it keeps people awake for ten nights instead of one. Aisha asked the Prophet what she should say if she found it, and he taught her a short prayer asking Allah, who loves to pardon, to pardon her. Peace until dawn.
screen: `WE REVEALED IT ON THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `THE ANGELS AND THE SPIRIT DESCEND.` · `THE ODD NIGHTS OF THE LAST TEN.` · then, large: `PEACE UNTIL DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for a coming morning: wake a little before dawn, and sit in the dark. No phone. For now, try a small version. Close your eyes, or dim the lights. Picture the sky just before sunrise, very still. Let the word salam, peace, rest on each out-breath. If you pray, you can ask for pardon in your own words, as Aisha was taught. Stay in the dark, and let it be peaceful. The bell holds the time.
Al-Qadr. Power and decree: the night the Qur'an was first revealed, better than a thousand months, peace until dawn. Today's word.
Your line: peace until dawn. Tonight, before sleep, let the last thing you do be quiet: no screen, no argument, just a minute of peace in the dark. Day one hundred eighty.

181.title: Al-'Alaq: the first words
181.hook: read, in the name of your Lord who created you from a clinging clot, who taught by the pen (96:1–5)
181.howItsDone: Muslims learn the story of the first revelation in the cave of Hira as part of the Prophet's life; the opening verses of Surah al-'Alaq are recited in the prayers and often quoted to honor learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Qadr, the night the Qur'an was first revealed. Your line was peace until dawn. Did you end the night with a quiet minute in the dark? Day one hundred eighty-one.

A cave, high on a mountain outside Mecca, just big enough for one person to sit. A man of about forty climbs up there often, to be alone, to think, to turn toward God, with food his wife Khadijah has packed. One night, according to Muslim tradition in the month of Ramadan, someone else is in the cave. Yesterday we heard about that night. Today we hear the words that were actually spoken in it: the first words of the Qur'an to be revealed. Today: Al-'Alaq, the first words.
screen: `A CAVE ON A MOUNTAIN.` → `SOMEONE ELSE IS IN THE CAVE.` → `THE FIRST WORDS REVEALED.`

segments.voice: The story is told by Aisha in the opening pages of Sahih al-Bukhari. The angel Jibril came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave of Hira and said one word: iqra'. Read, or recite. The Prophet answered: I am not a reader. The angel pressed him tight, until he could bear no more, and said again: read. Three times. And then came these words, in Pickthall's translation: Read: In the name of thy Lord who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous, Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not. 'Alaq, the word the surah is named for, means something that clings. Pickthall says clot; many translators today prefer a clinging thing, and scholars discuss the range. The point is the contrast: a human begins as something tiny and clinging, and is taught what he did not know. And notice the pen. The first revelation to a man who said I am not a reader is about reading and writing. In the Qur'an's very first lines, knowledge is a gift from Allah. The Prophet came down the mountain shaking and went home to Khadijah and said: cover me, cover me. She wrapped him up, listened, and told him: Allah would never disgrace you. You keep ties with family, you help the weak, you honor guests, you stand by people in hardship. The first person to believe him was the person who knew him best. Taught by the pen.
screen: `IQRA' — READ.` · `I AM NOT A READER.` · `A CLINGING THING, TAUGHT WHAT IT KNEW NOT.` · `COVER ME — AND KHADIJAH DID.` · then, large: `TAUGHT BY THE PEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line by hand. Find a pen and any paper, a receipt, the back of an envelope. If you can't right now, trace the letters with a finger on your palm. Write one thing you learned this week that you didn't know before. Go slowly. Feel the pen move. Then sit with it. Somebody taught you that, or something did. Notice where knowledge comes from. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Alaq. The clinging thing, the name of Surah ninety-six, whose first five verses were the first of the Qur'an revealed. Today's word.
Your line: taught by the pen. Write one line by hand today, on paper, and keep it. Let it remind you that everything you know, you were taught. Day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: Al-'Alaq: the one who forbids
182.hook: the man who forbids a servant to pray, and the command to bow and draw near (96:9–19)
182.tomorrow: At-Tin: the fig and the olive
182.howItsDone: When Muslims recite or hear 96:19 many perform a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilawah); in the daily prayers, the prostration is often called the moment of greatest nearness to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Alaq, the first words in the cave: read. Your line was taught by the pen. Did you write one line by hand, and what did you write? Day one hundred eighty-two.

Picture the Ka'bah in Mecca, in the early years. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is praying there, in the open, bowing, then putting his forehead on the ground. A powerful man of Quraysh is watching, and he's furious. He tells his friends: if I see Muhammad with his face in the dust again, I'll step on his neck. Someone who wants to stop another person from praying. The rest of Surah al-'Alaq, after the first five verses, is about this man, and about what the one praying should do. Today: Al-'Alaq, the one who forbids.

segments.voice: The surah turns from the pen to a warning: truly, the human being oversteps when he sees himself as self-sufficient. Then: have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays? The man isn't named in the surah. Commentators, and a hadith in Sahih Muslim, identify him as Abu Jahl, one of the Prophet's fiercest opponents. The hadith says he came forward to carry out his threat, and then suddenly drew back, shielding himself with his hands. Asked why, he said he'd seen between himself and the Prophet a trench of fire, and terror, and wings. The surah asks him questions: what if the one praying is rightly guided? What if he commands goodness? Doesn't he know that Allah sees? And then the last verse, which tells the one praying what to do. In Pickthall's translation: Nay! Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near. Not fight him. Not argue. Not hide. Bow down, and come closer. It's one of the verses where Muslims traditionally prostrate when they recite it. And it lines up with a hadith in Muslim: the closest a servant is to his Lord is while in prostration. So the lowest position of the body is the nearest point to Allah. The man who wanted to push a face into the dust didn't understand: that's exactly where the nearness is. And that closes a week that began with the quake and an atom of good, and moved through the earth's report, the clear proof, sincerity, the Night of Power, and now the cave and its first surah, whole.
screen: `HE SEES HIMSELF AS SELF-SUFFICIENT.` · `THE ONE WHO FORBIDS PRAYER.` · `OBEY NOT THOU HIM.` · `CLOSEST IN PROSTRATION.` · then, large: `BOW AND DRAW NEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you pray, you can make one prostration now, forehead to the ground, and stay there a few breaths longer than usual, drawing near. If you don't, try something like it: lower your head, gently, toward your knees or your hands, and let your whole body get small and still. Notice what it feels like to go low on purpose. Nothing to prove down there. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Alaq. The clinging thing, and the surah that ends: don't obey the one who forbids; bow down, and draw near. Today's word.
Your line: bow and draw near. When someone tries to shame you out of what you value today, don't fight it. Go lower, and closer. Day one hundred eighty-two.
